title: Demonstrate basic knowledge of the seed industry

lessons.title: Why seed matters and seed is alive
lessons.html:
Why seed matters and seed is alive

Almost all the food we eat starts with a seed. Maize for pap, wheat for bread, sunflower for cooking oil, beans, vegetables and pasture for cattle all grow from seed. If the seed is poor, the whole crop is poor. That is why the seed industry is so important for South Africa.

Who is in the seed industry?

  • Plant breeders make new cultivars that yield more or resist disease and drought.
  • Seed growers are farmers who grow seed crops under contract.
  • Seed companies clean, test, treat, pack and sell the seed.
  • Seed laboratories test seed quality.
  • Inspectors check fields and seed against the rules.
  • Dealers and co-ops sell seed to farmers.
  • Farmers plant the seed.

Seed is a living thing

A seed looks dry and dead, but inside it is a tiny living plant called the embryo. It also has stored food and a seed coat that protects it. The seed breathes very slowly. It can die if we treat it badly.

Things that harm seed:

  • Heat, for example bags left in the sun on a bakkie.
  • Moisture, for example a leaking roof or wet floor.
  • Rough handling, for example throwing or dropping bags. Seeds crack inside.
  • Insects and rats that eat the seed.
  • Age. Old seed grows less well.

Some seeds also have dormancy. This means they are alive but will not grow straight away. Nature uses this so seeds wait for the right season.

Because seed is alive, everybody who works with it must handle it gently, keep it cool and dry, and keep it away from chemicals that are not meant for it.

lessons.title: Seed quality and seed storage
lessons.html:
Seed quality and seed storage

A farmer buys seed for one reason: to get a good crop. Good quality seed has these parts.

Quality components

QualityWhat it means
Genetic purityThe seed is the cultivar named on the bag
Physical purityClean seed, no weed seed, stones or dust
GerminationMost seeds grow into normal plants
VigourSeeds come up strongly, even in hard conditions
MoistureSeed is dry enough to store safely
HealthFree from seed-borne diseases and pests

The seed laboratory tests these. The results go on the label on the bag.

Storing seed well

The two biggest enemies of stored seed are heat and moisture. A simple rule: keep seed cool and dry.

  • Store bags on pallets, not on the floor.
  • Keep a gap between stacks and the wall so you can check for rats and insects.
  • Keep the store clean. Sweep up spilt seed.
  • Keep the roof and doors in good order so rain cannot get in.
  • Use old seed first. This is called first in, first out.
  • Keep different cultivars apart and clearly labelled.

Treated seed

Many seeds are coated with a chemical to protect them. Treated seed is often coloured. Treated seed is poison. Never eat it and never feed it to animals or chickens. Wear gloves when you handle it and wash your hands after. Keep treated seed in a locked place, away from food. If someone swallows treated seed, take them and the bag label to a clinic or doctor at once.

lessons.title: Laws in the seed industry
lessons.html:
Laws in the seed industry

Because farmers depend on seed, the government has laws about seed. You do not need to know the laws in detail, but you must know that they exist and why.

Main laws

  • Plant Improvement Act: sets rules for selling seed of many crops, including registration of cultivars, seed quality standards, labelling and seed certification.
  • Plant Breeders' Rights Act: protects new cultivars. A breeder who made a new cultivar owns rights to it, like a patent. Others may not multiply and sell it without permission.
  • Act 36 of 1947 (Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act): controls the chemicals used to treat seed.
  • Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993: protects workers in seed stores, plants and fields.

What this means for you

  • Labels must be correct. Never swap labels or put seed in a bag with the wrong label.
  • Keep cultivars separate. Mixing them breaks the rules and harms the farmer.
  • Do not take seed of protected cultivars to plant or sell yourself.
  • Handle treated seed safely and keep it locked away.
  • Report anything that looks wrong to your supervisor, for example damaged labels or mixed bags.

Organisations

The Department of Agriculture is responsible for these laws. The South African National Seed Organisation (SANSOR) represents the seed industry and helps run seed certification.

Key points

  • Seed is the start of almost all food crops.
  • Seed is alive; heat, moisture and rough handling kill it.
  • Good seed is pure, clean, germinates well and is healthy.
  • Store seed cool and dry, on pallets, first in first out.
  • Laws protect farmers, breeders and workers; labels must always be correct.
